summary.text: Early inscriptional forms of 牛 are interpreted as emphasizing an ox’s head and horns; the graph was used for the animal, ox or cattle. The selected seal-style glyph is a modern rendering of a later form, not evidence for the earliest forms.

formation.text: Pictographic: paleographic accounts interpret early oracle-bone and bronze forms as a frontal ox head with horns; some bronze forms are described as including ears, eyes, and nose. This interpretation concerns early forms and does not imply that every later form preserves a clear picture.

history.text: The transmitted Shuowen description mentions horns, head, and a tail or raised-back feature, and glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. Duan Yucai later offers a different interpretation based on the animal’s work and patterns. These are lexicographic interpretations, not independent evidence for the graph’s origin.

Oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal forms are listed. The selected seal-style glyph is a modern rendering of a later form; neither it nor the listed form classes establishes a dated sequence or the earliest surviving specimen.
Use for cattle and personal-name use are both reported in bronze inscriptions, though the cited examples do not establish when either use began.

uncertainties.text: The head-and-horns pictographic analysis is supported for early forms, but the earliest securely dated specimen is unresolved. No competing formation or specific graphic corruption is documented in the cited accounts.
A modern dictionary also lists figurative stubbornness, star-name, zodiac, calendar, and surname uses. Their dates and connections to the animal sense are unresolved.

Supplied local data records Mandarin niú and Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese ngjuw and Old Chinese *[ŋ]ʷə. The character-specific Unihan record could not be accessed; these readings do not establish graphic formation, and 牛 is not analyzed as a phonetic component.

senses.text: The graph is interpreted as depicting the animal, and 牛 is reported in an inscription referring to cattle. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unresolved; this is the earliest supported sense, not a dated first use.

senses.period: Shuowen Jiezi; date of use not established here
senses.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. This dictionary gloss does not establish a separate earlier sense or the graph’s original meaning.
Personal-name use is reported in bronze inscriptions; the examples are not individually dated here.
A modern dictionary lists this figurative sense, but its date and development from the animal sense are unresolved.
A modern dictionary lists a lunar-mansion sense; its chronology and development are unresolved.
A modern dictionary lists a zodiac use; its chronology and relation to the animal sense are unresolved.
A modern dictionary lists this use, but its chronology and development are unresolved.
A modern dictionary lists surname use, but its date and development are unresolved.

limitations.text: No dated corpus of written senses establishes the chronology or semantic connections among the animal, figurative, astronomical, calendar, zodiac, and surname uses.

overview.text: Early forms of 牛 are interpreted as pictures emphasizing an ox’s head and horns. The character names the animal, meaning ox or cattle.
